questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a capital reserve?
options: A reserve that has not arisen from trading profit and cannot be distributed as a cash dividend
A reserve created from trading profit that may be paid out as a dividend
The cash a company holds to meet unexpected costs
The nominal value of the shares a company has issued
questions.why: Capital reserves such as share premium and revaluation reserve do not represent realised trading profit, so they cannot be paid out in cash.
whyNot: That is a revenue reserve.
That is a cash balance, not a reserve.
That is issued share capital.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a revenue reserve?
options: General reserve
Share premium
Revaluation reserve
Capital redemption reserve
questions.why: A general reserve is created by transferring retained earnings, so it is a revenue reserve and can be transferred back and distributed.
whyNot: Share premium arises on issuing shares above nominal value, so it is a capital reserve.
A revaluation reserve arises from restating an asset, not from trading, so it is a capital reserve.
A capital redemption reserve is created to keep capital intact, and is a capital reserve.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines authorised share capital?
options: The maximum nominal value of shares the company may issue under its constitution
The nominal value of the shares actually issued to shareholders
The amount shareholders have been asked to pay
The market value of all the company's shares
questions.why: Authorised capital is the ceiling, and it appears as a disclosure note rather than on the face of the statement of financial position.
whyNot: That is issued share capital.
That is called-up share capital.
That is market capitalisation, which does not appear in the financial statements.

questions.stem: In which statement do dividends paid appear?
options: The statement of changes in equity
The statement of comprehensive income, as an expense
The statement of financial position, as a non-current liability
They do not appear in any financial statement
questions.why: A dividend is an appropriation of profit, not an expense, so it is shown as a deduction from retained earnings in the statement of changes in equity.
whyNot: Dividends are not an expense and never reduce profit for the year.
A dividend already paid is not a liability at all.
It appears in the statement of changes in equity and in the cash flow statement.

questions.stem: Where is debenture interest shown in the statement of comprehensive income?
options: As a finance cost, after operating profit
As an administrative expense, before operating profit
As an appropriation of profit, after taxation
It is not shown, because it is an equity distribution
questions.why: Debenture interest is a finance cost, deducted after operating profit to arrive at profit before tax.
whyNot: Treating it as an administrative expense distorts operating profit.
It is a cost of borrowing, not an appropriation like a dividend.
It is an expense of the company because a debenture holder is a lender.

questions.stem: A company issues 200,000 ordinary shares of $0.50 each at $1.40. How much is credited to share premium?
questions.why: Premium per share = 1.40 - 0.50 = $0.90. Share premium = 200,000 x 0.90 = $180,000.
whyNot: That is the total cash received, which must be split between capital and premium.
That is the amount credited to share capital, 200,000 x $0.50.
That halves the premium by using $0.35 per share in error.

questions.stem: A company makes a 1 for 4 bonus issue on 600,000 shares of $0.25 each. What is the entry?
options: Dr reserves $37,500; Cr share capital $37,500
Dr bank $37,500; Cr share capital $37,500
Dr reserves $150,000; Cr share capital $150,000
Dr share capital $37,500; Cr reserves $37,500
questions.why: Bonus shares = 600,000 / 4 = 150,000, at a nominal value of $0.25 = $37,500, funded by debiting a reserve.
whyNot: A bonus issue raises no cash, so the bank is not involved.
That uses 150,000 shares at $1 instead of at the $0.25 nominal value.
The entry is the other way round: share capital increases and the reserve falls.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true of a bonus issue?
options: It raises no cash and leaves total equity unchanged
It raises cash from existing shareholders
It increases total equity by the nominal value of the shares issued
It reduces the number of shares in issue
questions.why: A bonus issue converts reserves into share capital, so it changes the composition of equity without changing its total.
whyNot: That is a rights issue.
Total equity is unchanged, because one part of equity is debited and another credited.
It increases the number of shares in issue.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of a rights issue over a public offer of shares?
options: It is cheaper, needs no prospectus and protects existing shareholders from dilution
It raises more cash per share than a public offer
It does not increase the number of shares in issue
It avoids any obligation to pay future dividends
questions.why: A rights issue is offered to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings, which is administratively simpler and cheaper.
whyNot: The discount means it usually raises less per share than a public offer.
New shares are issued, so the share count rises.
Ordinary shares carry the same dividend expectations however they are issued.

questions.stem: Which statement about debentures compared with ordinary shares is correct?
options: Debenture interest must be paid even if there is no profit, while dividends need not be
Debenture holders vote at general meetings, while ordinary shareholders do not
Debenture interest is an appropriation of profit, while dividends are an expense
Debenture holders are paid after ordinary shareholders on liquidation
questions.why: Interest is a contractual obligation, which is precisely where the risk of high gearing comes from.
whyNot: Debenture holders are lenders and have no voting rights.
It is the reverse: interest is an expense and dividends are an appropriation.
Lenders rank ahead of all shareholders on liquidation.

questions.stem: Ordinary share capital is $400,000, reserves are $200,000, 8% debentures are $250,000 and 6% preference shares are $150,000. What is capital gearing?
questions.why: Fixed-return capital = 250,000 + 150,000 = $400,000. Total long-term capital = $1,000,000. Gearing = 40%.
whyNot: That includes only the debentures and omits the preference shares.
That uses a denominator of $1.2m or omits the reserves.
That is the proportion of equity, which is the complement of gearing.

questions.stem: Using the figures above, what are the annual fixed charges that must be met before any ordinary dividend?
questions.why: Debenture interest = 250,000 x 8% = $20,000. Preference dividend = 150,000 x 6% = $9,000. Total = $29,000.
whyNot: That is the debenture interest only.
That is the preference dividend only.
That applies 8% to both sources.

questions.stem: A company has high capital gearing. Which pair of consequences is correct?
options: Higher risk because interest is obligatory, and higher returns to ordinary shareholders in good years
Lower risk and lower returns to ordinary shareholders
Higher risk and no possibility of higher returns
No change in risk, because interest is tax deductible
questions.why: Fixed charges magnify outcomes in both directions: any surplus above the interest belongs entirely to the ordinary shareholders.
whyNot: Gearing raises risk rather than lowering it.
The potential for higher returns is the reason companies use debt.
Tax deductibility lowers the cost of debt but does not remove the obligation to pay it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a provision?
options: A liability of uncertain timing or amount, recognised where an obligation exists and can be reliably estimated
An amount set aside out of profit for a future expansion
A liability whose timing and amount are both known exactly
An amount deducted from an asset to show its reduced value
questions.why: The uncertainty over timing or amount is what distinguishes a provision from an accrual.
whyNot: That is a reserve, which is part of equity, not a liability.
That is an accrual.
That describes an allowance offset against an asset, such as an allowance for doubtful debts.

questions.stem: What is the role of the external auditor?
options: To give an independent opinion on whether the financial statements give a true and fair view
To prepare the financial statements on behalf of the directors
To guarantee that the figures in the statements are exactly correct
To certify that no fraud has taken place in the company
questions.why: The auditor provides an independent check that makes directors accountable to shareholders, which is its role in corporate governance.
whyNot: Preparing the statements is the directors' responsibility.
An audit gives reasonable assurance based on sampling, not a guarantee.
Detecting all fraud is neither the purpose nor within the scope of an audit.

questions.stem: Why must exceptional items be disclosed separately?
options: So users can judge the underlying performance that is likely to recur
Because they are not allowed to affect profit
Because they are always losses rather than gains
Because the auditor cannot verify them
questions.why: An item of unusual size or incidence would distort the trend if it were buried within operating expenses.
whyNot: They do affect profit; they are simply shown separately.
They can be gains, such as a large one-off disposal profit.
Verifiability is not the reason for separate disclosure.

questions.stem: Why must discontinued activities be shown separately from continuing activities?
options: A user forecasting future results needs to know which profits will recur
Discontinued activities are exempt from taxation
Discontinued activities cannot be audited
The law requires discontinued activities to be excluded from profit
questions.why: Separating them lets users see the performance of the operations the company will still have next year.
whyNot: There is no such tax exemption.
They are audited like any other part of the statements.
They are included in profit, shown separately.

questions.stem: Company A pays $720,000 for Company B, whose assets at fair value are $623,000 and whose liabilities assumed are $37,000. What is goodwill?
whyNot: That deducts the assets only and ignores the liabilities assumed.
That adds the liabilities to the net assets instead of deducting them from the assets.
That uses an incorrect net asset figure.

questions.stem: A purchaser pays for a company with 500,000 shares of $1 issued at $1.30. How is the consideration recorded?
options: Cr share capital $500,000 and Cr share premium $150,000
Cr share capital $650,000
Cr share capital $500,000 and Cr goodwill $150,000
Cr share premium $650,000
questions.why: Shares are credited to capital at nominal value, and the excess of $0.30 per share goes to share premium.
whyNot: Crediting the whole consideration to share capital is the most frequently penalised error in this topic.
Goodwill is an asset and is not credited with the premium.
Only the excess over nominal value goes to share premium.

questions.stem: How is purchased goodwill treated under current accounting standards?
options: Recognised as a non-current intangible asset and reviewed for impairment
Written off against profit immediately in the year of purchase
Amortised on a straight-line basis over a fixed 20-year life
Not recognised at all, because it cannot be measured
questions.why: A price was paid for it, so it is recognised, and it is written down only if a review shows its value has fallen.
whyNot: Immediate write-off is not the current treatment.
Straight-line amortisation over a set life is not required under current standards.
Purchased goodwill can be measured, unlike internally generated goodwill.

questions.stem: Which of the following rows in a statement of changes in equity must total nil?
options: A bonus issue and a transfer to the general reserve
Dividends paid and a share issue
Total comprehensive income and dividends paid
A rights issue and a revaluation gain
questions.why: Both simply move value between columns of equity, so the total column must be zero. A bonus issue row with a total is an error.
whyNot: Both of these change total equity: one reduces it and one increases it.
Both change total equity.
Both increase total equity.

questions.stem: Why is debt often described as cheaper than its headline interest rate suggests?
options: Interest is deductible against tax, while dividends are not
Interest does not have to be paid in a loss-making year
Debenture holders accept a lower return than they are promised
Debt does not have to be repaid
questions.why: The tax relief reduces the effective cost, which is one reason a company with stable profits will use some debt.
whyNot: Interest is contractual and must be paid whatever the result.
The contractual rate is what is paid.
Debentures are repayable on a stated date.
